seo.title: 30 Common Mistakes Smart Contract Auditors Make
seo.description: Avoid these 30 common mistakes that smart contract auditors make. From missing edge cases to report writing errors, improve your audit quality.

content.intro: Even experienced auditors make mistakes that can lead to missed vulnerabilities or inaccurate reports. Learn from these common pitfalls to improve your audit quality.

sections.heading: Preparation Mistakes
sections.description: Errors made before the actual code review begins.

items.title: Not reading the documentation first
items.description: Jumping straight into code without understanding intended behavior leads to false positives and missed business logic bugs.
items.impact: Miss context-dependent vulnerabilities
items.prevention: Spend first 10-15% of audit time on docs, specs, and similar protocol audits.

items.title: Unclear scope definition
items.description: Starting without clear scope leads to wasted time on out-of-scope contracts or missing in-scope dependencies.
items.impact: Inefficient time use and missed vulnerabilities
items.prevention: Get explicit scope confirmation in writing before starting any code review.

items.title: Skipping automated tool runs
items.description: Not running Slither, Mythril, or other tools because you think manual review is sufficient.
items.impact: Miss low-hanging fruit that tools catch instantly
items.prevention: Always run automated tools first. They catch issues you might overlook.

items.title: Not setting up the local environment
items.description: Reviewing code without being able to run tests or write PoCs limits vulnerability verification.
items.impact: Cannot verify findings with proof of concept
items.prevention: Clone repo and get tests passing before deep code review.

items.title: Underestimating audit time needed
items.description: Accepting tight deadlines leads to rushed reviews and missed vulnerabilities.
items.impact: Incomplete audit coverage
items.prevention: Use realistic time estimates. Complex DeFi needs 1000+ lines per day is aggressive.

sections.heading: Technical Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in vulnerability identification and analysis.

items.title: Focusing only on code, not economics
items.description: Missing economic exploits because you only look for code bugs, not incentive manipulation.
items.impact: Miss profitable exploits that don't require code bugs
items.prevention: Model economic attacks. Ask: how would someone profit from manipulating this?

items.title: Missing cross-contract reentrancy
items.description: Only checking for single-contract reentrancy when the protocol has multiple interacting contracts.
items.impact: Miss complex reentrancy paths
items.prevention: Map all external calls and check if any can re-enter other protocol contracts.

items.title: Ignoring external dependencies
items.description: Not reviewing how the contract interacts with external protocols like Uniswap, Aave, or Chainlink.
items.impact: Miss integration vulnerabilities
items.prevention: Review external call assumptions. Check for edge cases in integrated protocols.

items.title: Not testing edge cases
items.description: Only testing happy path scenarios without considering zero values, max values, or empty arrays.
items.impact: Miss boundary condition bugs
items.prevention: Systematically test all boundary conditions in critical functions.

items.title: Misunderstanding protocol assumptions
items.description: Making incorrect assumptions about how the protocol should work without verifying with the team.
items.impact: False positives that waste everyone's time
items.prevention: When unsure, ask the team. Document assumptions in your notes.

items.title: Missing read-only reentrancy
items.description: Not considering that view functions can return stale data during reentrancy.
items.impact: Miss reentrancy that affects external protocols
items.prevention: Check if other protocols read state during external calls.

sections.heading: Analysis Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in vulnerability assessment and severity rating.

items.title: Incorrect severity assessment
items.description: Rating findings too high or too low damages credibility and prioritization.
items.impact: Team ignores valid findings or panics over minor issues
items.prevention: Use consistent severity framework. High/Critical requires fund loss or protocol break.

items.title: Not writing proof of concept
items.description: Reporting theoretical vulnerabilities without proving they're exploitable.
items.impact: Invalid findings that cannot be reproduced
items.prevention: Write PoC for all medium+ findings. If you cannot exploit it, reconsider.

items.title: Missing the root cause
items.description: Reporting symptoms rather than underlying vulnerability leads to incomplete fixes.
items.impact: Fix addresses symptom but root cause remains exploitable
items.prevention: Always identify why the vulnerability exists, not just what it does.

items.title: Duplicate findings from different angles
items.description: Reporting the same underlying issue multiple times as separate findings.
items.impact: Inflated finding count, wastes team time reviewing duplicates
items.prevention: Before adding finding, check if it shares root cause with existing finding.

items.title: Missing attack prerequisites
items.description: Not clearly stating what conditions must exist for the attack to succeed.
items.impact: Overstated severity or invalid findings
items.prevention: Document all prerequisites: timing, capital, permissions, market conditions.

items.title: Ignoring gas costs in attack profitability
items.description: Reporting attacks that are unprofitable after gas costs are considered.
items.impact: Invalid economic exploits
items.prevention: Calculate full attack cost including gas and flash loan fees.

sections.heading: Report Writing Mistakes
sections.description: Errors in documenting and communicating findings.

items.title: Unclear vulnerability descriptions
items.description: Writing descriptions that only make sense to you, not the development team.
items.impact: Team cannot understand or fix the issue
items.prevention: Write for developers who did not audit. Include context and clear steps.

items.title: Missing code references
items.description: Not including specific line numbers and file paths for vulnerable code.
items.impact: Team cannot locate the vulnerable code
items.prevention: Include file path, line numbers, and relevant code snippets.

items.title: Vague recommendations
items.description: Suggesting fixes like 'add validation' without specifying what validation.
items.impact: Team implements incomplete fix
items.prevention: Provide specific, implementable fix recommendations with code examples.

items.title: Not explaining impact clearly
items.description: Technical description without business impact leaves team unsure how to prioritize.
items.impact: Critical issues may be deprioritized
items.prevention: Always explain: what can attacker do, how much can they steal, what breaks.

items.title: Forgetting to verify fixes
items.description: Not reviewing the fixes implemented for your findings.
items.impact: Incomplete or incorrect fixes deploy to mainnet
items.prevention: Review all fix commits. Verify root cause addressed, not just symptom.

items.title: Poor report organization
items.description: Dumping findings without logical organization or executive summary.
items.impact: Stakeholders cannot quickly understand risk exposure
items.prevention: Include executive summary, group by severity, provide statistics.

items.title: Working in isolation without team discussion
items.description: Not discussing potential findings with other auditors leads to missed insights.
items.impact: Lower quality audit, duplicate efforts
items.prevention: Schedule regular sync calls. Discuss interesting code paths and potential issues.

items.title: Not tracking time per area
items.description: Spending too much time on one area while neglecting others.
items.impact: Uneven coverage leaves blind spots
items.prevention: Track time spent per contract or area. Ensure balanced coverage.

items.title: Disclosing vulnerabilities inappropriately
items.description: Sharing findings publicly before the team has patched.
items.impact: Enable exploits, damage reputation, potential legal issues
items.prevention: Follow responsible disclosure. Never share details until fixed.

items.title: Not maintaining finding database
items.description: Each audit starts from scratch without use patterns from past audits.
items.impact: Slower audits, repeated mistakes
items.prevention: Maintain personal database of finding patterns and vulnerable code patterns.

items.title: Skipping the retest phase
items.description: Assuming fixes are correct without verification.
items.impact: Broken or incomplete fixes go to production
items.prevention: Always verify fixes address root cause and don't introduce new issues.

items.title: Ignoring test coverage gaps
items.description: Not reviewing what tests exist and what code paths remain untested.
items.impact: Critical paths may be untested, hiding bugs
items.prevention: Review test coverage. Flag untested code as higher risk.

items.title: Missing cross-protocol interactions
items.description: Auditing in isolation without considering how other protocols might interact.
items.impact: Composability attacks missed
items.prevention: Consider flash loan attack vectors and other protocol interactions.

items.title: Not tracking previous audits
items.description: Failing to review findings from previous audits of the same protocol.
items.impact: Re-introducing old vulnerabilities or missing recurring patterns
items.prevention: Always request and review previous audit reports.

proTips.tip: Keep a checklist of common vulnerabilities and check each one explicitly. Do not rely on memory.
Take breaks. Auditor fatigue causes missed findings. Fresh eyes catch more bugs.
Build relationships with protocol teams. Good communication improves audit quality for everyone.
Study every post-mortem. When a protocol gets exploited, understand exactly what the auditors missed.
Contribute to open-source security tools. Building tools deepens your understanding of vulnerability patterns.
